DIRECTOR'S DUTY OF CARE AND THE BUSINESS JUDGMENT RULE — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme, Inc.

PURPOSE AND SCOPE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This Information Sheet describes California Corporations Code section 309 — the statutory standard of care that governs how a director of a California corporation performs the duties of a director, the statutory right of a director to rely on information and reports from certain other sources in performing those duties, and the statutory consequence for a director who performs duties consistently with that standard and that reliance right. It is prepared with reference to Jordan Lee's service as a director of Acme, Inc. This Information Sheet is a general reference describing what section 309 provides; it does not evaluate, and is not evidence of, whether any specific decision, vote, or other conduct by Jordan Lee as a director of Acme, Inc. satisfied the standard of care described here, whether Jordan Lee was in fact entitled to rely on any specific information or report, or whether the liability protection described here would apply to any specific act or omission. Those are fact-specific questions this Information Sheet does not answer. This document treats section 309 as it applies to a California corporation's directors specifically, in more depth than this project's existing Founders' Agreement document, which addresses fiduciary duties only briefly and only as one comparison point among the different duties owed by partners, corporate directors, and LLC members or managers depending on which entity form founders have chosen.

THE STATUTORY STANDARD OF CARE FOR A DIRECTOR'S PERFORMANCE OF DUTIES
California law sets a single statutory standard for how a director of a California corporation must perform the duties of a director, including duties performed as a member of a board committee. The statute requires a director to act (1) in good faith; (2) in a manner the director believes to be in the best interests of the corporation and its shareholders; and (3) with the care, including reasonable inquiry, that an ordinarily prudent person in a like position would use under similar circumstances. This is the standard against which Jordan Lee's performance of duties as a director of Acme, Inc. is measured under California corporate law; this clause states the standard itself and does not evaluate whether any specific decision by Jordan Lee met it.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "A director shall perform the duties of a director, including duties as a member of any committee of the board upon which the director may serve, in good faith, in a manner such director believes to be in the best interests of the corporation and its shareholders and with such care, including reasonable inquiry, as an ordinarily prudent person in a like position would use under similar circumstances."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 309(a), California General Corporation Law, standard of care for a director's performance of duties (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=309.)
  Known gap: This is one California statute (Corporations Code section 309, subdivision (a)) and is offered as evidence of what that subdivision provides, not as a claim about which state's law governs any specific company or as a determination that any specific company is in fact organized as a California corporation. This clause does not address how California courts have applied or weighted the standard's three elements in a specific dispute, nor does it address a director's right to rely on others in satisfying this standard, which is covered in the following clauses quoting subdivision (b) of this same statutory section — the citations across this document's clauses are different subdivisions of the single statute, Corporations Code section 309, not independent sources corroborating one another.

THE STATUTORY RIGHT TO RELY ON OFFICERS, EXPERTS, AND BOARD COMMITTEES
In performing the duties described in the preceding clause, California law entitles a director to rely on information, opinions, reports, or statements — including financial statements and other financial data — that are prepared or presented by any of three categories of sources: (1) one or more officers or employees of the corporation whom the director believes to be reliable and competent in the matters presented; (2) counsel, independent accountants, or other persons as to matters the director believes to be within that person's professional or expert competence; or (3) a board committee on which the director does not serve, as to matters within that committee's designated authority, if the director believes the committee merits confidence. The statute attaches conditions to this reliance right, addressed in the following clause. This clause states which categories of sources Jordan Lee may rely on under the statute as a director of Acme, Inc.; it does not determine whether any specific officer, employee, professional, or committee that Jordan Lee in fact relied on falls within one of these categories.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "In performing the duties of a director, a director shall be entitled to rely on information, opinions, reports or statements, including financial statements and other financial data, in each case prepared or presented by any of the following: (1) One or more officers or employees of the corporation whom the director believes to be reliable and competent in the matters presented. (2) Counsel, independent accountants or other persons as to matters which the director believes to be within such person’s professional or expert competence. (3) A committee of the board upon which the director does not serve, as to matters within its designated authority, which committee the director believes to merit confidence, so long as, in any such case, the director acts in good faith, after reasonable inquiry when the need therefor is indicated by the circumstances and without knowledge that would cause such reliance to be unwarranted."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 309(b), California General Corporation Law, sources a director may rely on and the conditions attached (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=309.)
  Known gap: This is the same California statute as the preceding and following clauses in this document (Corporations Code section 309), quoting subdivision (b) in full, including its concluding conditions clause — it is not an independent source corroborating the standard-of-care clause or the liability-protection clause; all three quote different subdivisions of one statutory section. The statute lists three categories of permissible reliance and does not state whether that list is illustrative or exhaustive; this clause does not address whether reliance on a source outside these three categories could be supported under some legal theory outside section 309 itself.

CONDITIONS ON THE RELIANCE RIGHT, AND WHAT IT DOES NOT EXCUSE
The statutory right to rely on officers, experts, and board committees described in the preceding clause is not unconditional. California law makes reliance on any of the three categories of sources available only if the director acts in good faith, after reasonable inquiry when the circumstances indicate a need for it, and without knowledge that would make the reliance unwarranted. This means the reliance right does not excuse a director who reviews the information, opinion, report, or statement in question but who knows something that would make reliance on it unreasonable, and it does not excuse a director who fails to make a reasonable inquiry when the circumstances call for one. This clause states the statutory conditions themselves; it does not evaluate whether Jordan Lee, as a director of Acme, Inc., in fact acted in good faith, made a reasonable inquiry, or possessed knowledge that would make a specific instance of reliance unwarranted — those are fact-specific determinations this clause does not make.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "so long as, in any such case, the director acts in good faith, after reasonable inquiry when the need therefor is indicated by the circumstances and without knowledge that would cause such reliance to be unwarranted."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 309(b), California General Corporation Law, conditions attached to a director's statutory reliance right (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=309.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes only the concluding conditions sentence of Corporations Code section 309, subdivision (b) — the same subdivision (b) quoted in full, including this identical sentence, in the preceding clause. It is isolated here only to highlight the conditions specifically; it is not an independent additional source, and the two clauses' citations should not be read as corroborating one another rather than being the same statutory text. The statute does not define "reasonable inquiry" or specify what circumstances "indicate" a need for it, and this clause does not supply those definitions.

THE LIABILITY PROTECTION FOR A DIRECTOR WHO MEETS THE STANDARD
California law provides that a person who performs the duties of a director consistently with the standard of care and the reliance right described in the preceding clauses has no liability based on any alleged failure to discharge that person's obligations as a director. This is the statutory codification of what is commonly referred to as business judgment rule protection for a California corporate director: a director who satisfies the good-faith, best-interests, and ordinarily-prudent-person standard (and, where applicable, the conditions on reliance) is not liable merely because a decision, in hindsight, turned out badly for the corporation. The statute separately notes that a corporation's liability for monetary damages against a director may also be eliminated or limited in the corporation's articles, to the extent a different statute (Corporations Code section 204, subdivision (a), paragraph (10)) permits — a distinct, additional protection this clause does not itself describe in detail. This clause states the statutory liability protection itself; it does not determine whether Jordan Lee's conduct as a director of Acme, Inc. in fact met the standard described in the preceding clauses, or whether Acme, Inc.'s articles of incorporation contain any exculpatory provision of the kind referenced here.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "A person who performs the duties of a director in accordance with subdivisions (a) and (b) shall have no liability based upon any alleged failure to discharge the person’s obligations as a director. In addition, the liability of a director for monetary damages may be eliminated or limited in a corporation’s articles to the extent provided in paragraph (10) of subdivision (a) of Section 204."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 309(c), California General Corporation Law, liability protection for a director who meets the standard of subdivisions (a) and (b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=309.)
  Known gap: This is the same California statute as the two preceding authority clauses (Corporations Code section 309), quoting subdivision (c) — not an independent source corroborating them. This clause references, but does not independently fetch, quote, or verify, Corporations Code section 204, subdivision (a), paragraph (10) (the separate statute governing exculpatory provisions in a corporation's articles); that cross-reference is stated only because it appears within the verified text of section 309(c) itself, and readers should consult section 204 directly rather than relying on this clause for its substance. This clause also does not address the separate, non-statutory common-law business judgment rule as California courts have applied it in specific disputes (for example, the deference given to a board's decision absent fraud, illegality, or a conflict of interest) — no case law is cited or verified anywhere in this document; this document is limited to the verified statutory text of section 309.

CERTIFICATION
I certify that the description of California Corporations Code section 309 in this Information Sheet reflects the statutory text as in effect on the date below, and that this Information Sheet is a general informational reference regarding Jordan Lee's service as a director of Acme, Inc., not legal advice about, or a determination of, whether any specific act or omission by Jordan Lee satisfied the standard of care, qualified for the statutory reliance right, or is protected from liability under the statute described above.

Executed on September 3, 2026 at Oakland, California.
